messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am hoping to use the geomorph package to undertake further analyses.

I have used the r package 'Morpho' to slide my semilandmarks on curves and surfaces using the slider3d function on my 3D landmark array. After that, I put the new data (slid landmark configurations) into a data array to use for further analyses (using dataslide from the slider3d output).

I am just wanting to please confirm if it is appropriate for me to use this new data array (with semilandmarks already slid) in further analyses undertaken in geomorph?

For example, using gpagen, because semilandmarks are already slid (and I am using this new data array with semilandmarks having already undergone sliding) I therefore do not need to include the arguments curves or surfaces? Is this correct? Are there any issues that geomorph might have with analyses if I do not undertake sliding in this package?

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Kate

messages.body_plain:
Kate,

Once GPA is performed, with or without sliding landmarks, and regardless of function, the data can be analyzed as if the coordinates are now fixed.  Yes, it is appropriate, given your trust in the GPA performed.

Note that you can use gpagen to slide surface and curve semilandmarks.  One chief difference compared to slider3d is that if the defaults of that function are used, it will arrest GPA iterations early, if there is an increase in the convergence criterion.  But as the criterion is not guaranteed to decay with sliding semilandmarks (it will bounce around), it is not wise to just accept the default.  In gpagen, one defines the maximum number of iterations to perform if convergence is not found (and it almost never is with sliding semilandmarks).  Regardless of function, one should check how well GPA converged with different sets of iterations.

Best,
Mike

I revisited this thread recently and wish to better understand Mike's comment: for clustering of a matrix of RV coefficients, where each element of the matrix is the RV value calculated for each pair of landmarks, the key issue is the separate standardization for each lm pair when deriving the  matrix of RV coefficients.

1. It is true that GPA minimizes variance globally not locally. But when comparing the entries of the matrix of RV coefficients calculated after GPA, why do we need to use a common value to standardize the numerators? It is true that for two landmark pairs (pair 1: landmark A- landmark B; pair 2: lm C- lm D), when the RV numerators for pair 1 and pair 2 are the same but the denominator for pair 1 is larger than that for pair 2, RV for pair 1 will be lower than RV for pair 2. I understand this difference in denominator (landmark variance after GPA) may be partly due to the effect of GPA. So it is no longer the variance of original landmarks, but variance of Procrustes coordinates. But what we are investigating is clusters of SHAPE of the object , not clusters of the ORIGINAL CONFIGURATION of the object (let me know if I am wrong). So we need to derive shape variables, and we need GPA. I am not sure how the fact that "GPA minimizes variance globally not locally" makes it inappropriate to do separate standardization after GPA when deriving the matrix of RV coefficients for cluster analysis aiming to obtain modules of shape. I seem to be asking 2 Qs: a) whether we should normally aim for deriving modules for the original configurations or modules for shape of the configuration; b) How "GPA minimizes variance globally not locally" makes it inappropriate to do separate standardization. Maybe these 2 Qs are internally connected. I kind of get mixed up.

2. Mike's explanation has been focused on the issue of separate standardization, which concerns the denominators being different. But GPA should make both variance and covariance of original landmarks and Procrustes coordinates different. Why not worried about the numerator? Is it because GPA does not change overall variance of the configuration, so sum of squared singular values remain unchanged, eventhough for each landmark, the variance changes?

Thank you very much for this further clarification.

Lv

> I have two comments to make as a follow-up.  Thanks to Kieran for a detailed private message that clears up what the purpose of the methods used in the papers he provided.  I feel I can comment more specifically on what was intended and whether it was correct.  I have two comments to make.
>
> First, the purpose of the analysis is not a test but rather a descriptive procedure.  For a configuration of p points in k dimensions, find the RV coefficient between all pairs of p_i, p_j landmarks and record this value in a matrix.  All values would be positive and presumably measure the strength of association between landmarks.  One could image the matrix like a heat map and find the areas in the configuration where there are clusters of highly associated points.  On the surface this seems like a good tool, and because it uses portions of a covariance matrix that have been established after GPA, it is not a one-at-a-time kind of landmark analysis.
>
> However this approach is fundamentally flawed (even if it was published).  The RV coefficient standardizes covariances by joint variances and because those variances will vary among landmark pairs, the method of standardization is incommensurate across landmarks.  It is possible to find landmarks with higher covariation but lower correlation because the pairs have different landmark variances, which should be taken also with a grain of salt since they are portions of configurations from a procedure that intended to minimize variance globally, not locally.
>
> The numerator of each RV coefficient is the sum of squared singular values in the between-landmark covariances.  The denominators are the products of the sums of eigenvalues within landmark covariance matrices.  I might buy that this procedure is a valid thing to do if only the numerator squared singular values were used for comparative purposes, or they were standardized by a common value, like the sum of eigenvalues for the entire matrix.  But with RV coefficients estimated without regard to other landmarks, spurious results should be typical.
>
> Second comment, speaking of spurious results, I would really like to start a campaign that GPA does not induce spurious results.  I know some of our colleagues have published papers about the peril of GM data and test of modularity/integration but I feel there has been a tendency to blame the messenger for providing data that already had true spatial covariances that were not independent before GPA.  Having many anatomical points in close proximity, perhaps for the same structure, means having strong spatial covariances among those points.  GPA does not create those covariances.  If anything, GPA might buffer their true strength by finding means of those points after rotation, thus making the landmarks less spatially related for the mean than for any single configuration.
>
> We need to let go of thinking that data subjected to GPA come out with induced modularity or integration.  It will be possible, however, to misinterpret modularity and integration by performing analyses on parts of configurations rather than the entire configurations.  Finding the RV coefficient by landmark pairs is one way to do this.  I have no qualms with finding the eigenvalues of cross-products by pair, however, as long as they come from data from the same GPA.  This does not change the global solution.  The p * (p - 1) / 2 separate standardization methods in the RV coefficients does.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

> > On Feb 22, 2023, at 9:30 AM, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I think there might be some conflating of the RV coefficient as a descriptive statistic and as a test statistic in a test of modularity.  It *is* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from a landmark configuration comprising two modules, one of which contains only one landmark.  The one-landmark covariance matrix would be a 2 x 2 matrix for 2d landmarks or a 3 x 3 matrix for 3d landmarks, so covariances do exist in these matrices.  But even this is a distraction.  The RV coefficient was introduced by Escoufier in 1973, not with landmarks in mind.  It *is also* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from two variables, each with covariances matrices that are single values: variances.  The RV coefficient should be the square of the correlation coefficient between the variables in such cases, which is why the RV coefficient has intuitive appeal as a multivariate generalization of correlation.
> >
> > However, a test of modularity using the RV coefficient as a test statistic randomizes combinations of landmarks within modules, which is the same as randomizing the locations of variances and covariances within a covariance matrix, without changing the covariances.  But the randomization is constrained such that x, y, and possibly z covariances within landmarks  cannot be changed (the coordinates are not randomized between landmarks).  Although one *could* calculate an RV coefficient in every random permutation that assigns a landmark randomly to be a one-landmark module, the distribution of RV coefficients from this process would be meaningless for evaluating any null hypothesis about modularity.  If the point is to illustrate the meaninglessness from a simulation, I would argue that the simulation experiment is not needed, as its purpose is invalid, based on first principles.
> >
> > Dean’s point was a simulation forced to find RV coefficients from random one-landmark modules will produce distributions fraught with misinterpretation.  Unless there is at least one pair of landmarks — and even then, be careful of spurious results! — a test of modularity just should not be considered.  The RV coefficient might still be a descriptive statistic, but it cannot be considered an appropriate test statistic in tests involving one-landmark modules.

Dear Kieran,

I hope this much is clear.  The numerator of the RV coefficient measures the summed squared covariances between matrices.  If the two matrices are variables for two landmarks.  The numerator is an unstandardized strength of association between landmarks, since the summed squared covariances is always positive.

The RV coefficient is the summed squared covariances divided by the square root of the product of the variances (the summed squared variances and covariances within landmarks).  This value varies by landmark pairings.

If a map of RV coefficients purports to show areas of high covariation, the measure of association should be reliable.  I will demonstrate what I tried to explain before, using the pupfish data in geomorph.

Here is the script:

library(geomorph)
data(pupfish)

rv <- function(x, y){ # assumes data are centered

  Sx <- crossprod(x)
  Sy <- crossprod(y)
  num <- sum(crossprod(x, y)^2)
  RV <- num / sqrt(sum(Sx^2) * sum(Sy^2))
  c(summedSqCov = num, RV = RV)
}

p <- GPA$p
lm.combos <- combn(p, 2)

Result <- t(sapply(1:ncol(lm.combos), function(j){
  a <- lm.combos[1, j]
  b <- lm.combos[2, j]
  coords <- pupfish$coords[c(a, b), , ]
  Y <- scale(two.d.array(coords), scale = FALSE)
  rv(Y[, 1:2], Y[, 3:4])
}))

plot(Result, pch = 16)

Here is the plot:

As you can see, there are pairs of landmarks with low covariation but high RV, and vice versa.  Do you not consider that a problem?

Mike

> > I have two comments to make as a follow-up.  Thanks to Kieran for a detailed private message that clears up what the purpose of the methods used in the papers he provided.  I feel I can comment more specifically on what was intended and whether it was correct.  I have two comments to make.
> >
> > First, the purpose of the analysis is not a test but rather a descriptive procedure.  For a configuration of p points in k dimensions, find the RV coefficient between all pairs of p_i, p_j landmarks and record this value in a matrix.  All values would be positive and presumably measure the strength of association between landmarks.  One could image the matrix like a heat map and find the areas in the configuration where there are clusters of highly associated points.  On the surface this seems like a good tool, and because it uses portions of a covariance matrix that have been established after GPA, it is not a one-at-a-time kind of landmark analysis.
> >
> > However this approach is fundamentally flawed (even if it was published).  The RV coefficient standardizes covariances by joint variances and because those variances will vary among landmark pairs, the method of standardization is incommensurate across landmarks.  It is possible to find landmarks with higher covariation but lower correlation because the pairs have different landmark variances, which should be taken also with a grain of salt since they are portions of configurations from a procedure that intended to minimize variance globally, not locally.
> >
> > The numerator of each RV coefficient is the sum of squared singular values in the between-landmark covariances.  The denominators are the products of the sums of eigenvalues within landmark covariance matrices.  I might buy that this procedure is a valid thing to do if only the numerator squared singular values were used for comparative purposes, or they were standardized by a common value, like the sum of eigenvalues for the entire matrix.  But with RV coefficients estimated without regard to other landmarks, spurious results should be typical.
> >
> > Second comment, speaking of spurious results, I would really like to start a campaign that GPA does not induce spurious results.  I know some of our colleagues have published papers about the peril of GM data and test of modularity/integration but I feel there has been a tendency to blame the messenger for providing data that already had true spatial covariances that were not independent before GPA.  Having many anatomical points in close proximity, perhaps for the same structure, means having strong spatial covariances among those points.  GPA does not create those covariances.  If anything, GPA might buffer their true strength by finding means of those points after rotation, thus making the landmarks less spatially related for the mean than for any single configuration.
> >
> > We need to let go of thinking that data subjected to GPA come out with induced modularity or integration.  It will be possible, however, to misinterpret modularity and integration by performing analyses on parts of configurations rather than the entire configurations.  Finding the RV coefficient by landmark pairs is one way to do this.  I have no qualms with finding the eigenvalues of cross-products by pair, however, as long as they come from data from the same GPA.  This does not change the global solution.  The p * (p - 1) / 2 separate standardization methods in the RV coefficients does.
> >

> > > I think there might be some conflating of the RV coefficient as a descriptive statistic and as a test statistic in a test of modularity.  It *is* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from a landmark configuration comprising two modules, one of which contains only one landmark.  The one-landmark covariance matrix would be a 2 x 2 matrix for 2d landmarks or a 3 x 3 matrix for 3d landmarks, so covariances do exist in these matrices.  But even this is a distraction.  The RV coefficient was introduced by Escoufier in 1973, not with landmarks in mind.  It *is also* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from two variables, each with covariances matrices that are single values: variances.  The RV coefficient should be the square of the correlation coefficient between the variables in such cases, which is why the RV coefficient has intuitive appeal as a multivariate generalization of correlation.
> > >
> > > However, a test of modularity using the RV coefficient as a test statistic randomizes combinations of landmarks within modules, which is the same as randomizing the locations of variances and covariances within a covariance matrix, without changing the covariances.  But the randomization is constrained such that x, y, and possibly z covariances within landmarks  cannot be changed (the coordinates are not randomized between landmarks).  Although one *could* calculate an RV coefficient in every random permutation that assigns a landmark randomly to be a one-landmark module, the distribution of RV coefficients from this process would be meaningless for evaluating any null hypothesis about modularity.  If the point is to illustrate the meaninglessness from a simulation, I would argue that the simulation experiment is not needed, as its purpose is invalid, based on first principles.
> > >
> > > Dean’s point was a simulation forced to find RV coefficients from random one-landmark modules will produce distributions fraught with misinterpretation.  Unless there is at least one pair of landmarks — and even then, be careful of spurious results! — a test of modularity just should not be considered.  The RV coefficient might still be a descriptive statistic, but it cannot be considered an appropriate test statistic in tests involving one-landmark modules.

Dear Prof. Mike,

Thank you for the response. My question is exactly about taking your response in Feb further and ask "Do I really consider that a problem?".

Here is my reasoning why separate standardization indeed is a problem:

If we are comparing the association between body height and weight and between icecream sale and day-time temperature, we do no stop at covariance but rather scale the covariance by sqrt of product of variance since the variables are not on the same scale. But for Procrustes coordinates, they are on the same scale. The scaling step in RV coef does not help much as it does in the icecream example but complicates the issue since GPA influences landmark covariance differntially as a global approach to minize overall variance.

If the above reasoning is in the correct direction, it is implicitly suggesting that we are trying to recover clusters of the original configurations. So we are worried about the impact of changing landmark covariance after GPA. But what if we are to identify clusters of shape of the original configurations after GPA? Some background on this question is from the following statement in page 123 of Klingenberg's 2021 paper "How Exactly Did the Nose Get That Long?": "If the goal is to find a method that represents the covariance structure of the original data, Procrustes superimposition is inherently a poor choice of method because it focuses on shape only and omits all non-shape components of variation. If the goal of the simulation is to extract shape variation, discrepancies between the simulated data and the Procrustes-superimposed configurations are not a problem." This seems to suggest if our aim is to find clusters based on shape data, then the fact that GPA changes landmark variances differentially does not matter much. This is where I get confused.

Thank you for your interest!

On Sunday 17 December 2023 at 03:05:37 UTC+8 mlco...@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear Kieran,
>
> I hope this much is clear.  The numerator of the RV coefficient measures the summed squared covariances between matrices.  If the two matrices are variables for two landmarks.  The numerator is an unstandardized strength of association between landmarks, since the summed squared covariances is always positive.
>
> The RV coefficient is the summed squared covariances divided by the square root of the product of the variances (the summed squared variances and covariances within landmarks).  This value varies by landmark pairings.
>
> If a map of RV coefficients purports to show areas of high covariation, the measure of association should be reliable.  I will demonstrate what I tried to explain before, using the pupfish data in geomorph.
>
> Here is the script:
>
> library(geomorph)
> data(pupfish)
>
> rv <- function(x, y){ # assumes data are centered
>
>   Sx <- crossprod(x)
>   Sy <- crossprod(y)
>   num <- sum(crossprod(x, y)^2)
>   RV <- num / sqrt(sum(Sx^2) * sum(Sy^2))
>   c(summedSqCov = num, RV = RV)
> }
>
> p <- GPA$p
> lm.combos <- combn(p, 2)
>
> Result <- t(sapply(1:ncol(lm.combos), function(j){
>   a <- lm.combos[1, j]
>   b <- lm.combos[2, j]
>   coords <- pupfish$coords[c(a, b), , ]
>   Y <- scale(two.d.array(coords), scale = FALSE)
>   rv(Y[, 1:2], Y[, 3:4])
> }))
>
> plot(Result, pch = 16)
>
> Here is the plot:
>
>
> As you can see, there are pairs of landmarks with low covariation but high RV, and vice versa.  Do you not consider that a problem?
>
> Mike

> >

I understand this difference in denominator (landmark variance after GPA) may be partly due to the effect of GPA. So it is no longer the variance of original landmarks, but variance of Procrustes coordinates. But what we are investigating is clusters of SHAPE of the object , not clusters of the ORIGINAL CONFIGURATION of the object (let me know if I am wrong). So we need to derive shape variables, and we need GPA. I am not sure how the fact that "GPA minimizes variance globally not locally" makes it inappropriate to do separate standardization after GPA when deriving the matrix of RV coefficients for cluster analysis aiming to obtain modules of shape. I seem to be asking 2 Qs: a) whether we should normally aim for deriving modules for the original configurations or modules for shape of the configuration; b) How "GPA minimizes variance globally not locally" makes it inappropriate to do separate standardization. Maybe these 2 Qs are internally connected. I kind of get mixed up.

But GPA should make both variance and covariance of original landmarks and Procrustes coordinates different. Why not worried about the numerator? > > On Thursday 23 February 2023 at 01:03:44 UTC+8 mlco...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > I have two comments to make as a follow-up.  Thanks to Kieran for a detailed private message that clears up what the purpose of the methods used in the papers he provided.  I feel I can comment more specifically on what was intended and whether it was correct.  I have two comments to make.
> > >
> > > First, the purpose of the analysis is not a test but rather a descriptive procedure.  For a configuration of p points in k dimensions, find the RV coefficient between all pairs of p_i, p_j landmarks and record this value in a matrix.  All values would be positive and presumably measure the strength of association between landmarks.  One could image the matrix like a heat map and find the areas in the configuration where there are clusters of highly associated points.  On the surface this seems like a good tool, and because it uses portions of a covariance matrix that have been established after GPA, it is not a one-at-a-time kind of landmark analysis.
> > >
> > > However this approach is fundamentally flawed (even if it was published).  The RV coefficient standardizes covariances by joint variances and because those variances will vary among landmark pairs, the method of standardization is incommensurate across landmarks.  It is possible to find landmarks with higher covariation but lower correlation because the pairs have different landmark variances, which should be taken also with a grain of salt since they are portions of configurations from a procedure that intended to minimize variance globally, not locally.
> > >
> > > The numerator of each RV coefficient is the sum of squared singular values in the between-landmark covariances.  The denominators are the products of the sums of eigenvalues within landmark covariance matrices.  I might buy that this procedure is a valid thing to do if only the numerator squared singular values were used for comparative purposes, or they were standardized by a common value, like the sum of eigenvalues for the entire matrix.  But with RV coefficients estimated without regard to other landmarks, spurious results should be typical.
> > >
> > > Second comment, speaking of spurious results, I would really like to start a campaign that GPA does not induce spurious results.  I know some of our colleagues have published papers about the peril of GM data and test of modularity/integration but I feel there has been a tendency to blame the messenger for providing data that already had true spatial covariances that were not independent before GPA.  Having many anatomical points in close proximity, perhaps for the same structure, means having strong spatial covariances among those points.  GPA does not create those covariances.  If anything, GPA might buffer their true strength by finding means of those points after rotation, thus making the landmarks less spatially related for the mean than for any single configuration.
> > >
> > > We need to let go of thinking that data subjected to GPA come out with induced modularity or integration.  It will be possible, however, to misinterpret modularity and integration by performing analyses on parts of configurations rather than the entire configurations.  Finding the RV coefficient by landmark pairs is one way to do this.  I have no qualms with finding the eigenvalues of cross-products by pair, however, as long as they come from data from the same GPA.  This does not change the global solution.  The p * (p - 1) / 2 separate standardization methods in the RV coefficients does.
> > >
> > > Cheers!
> > > Mike
> > >
> > >
> > > > On Feb 22, 2023, at 9:30 AM, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I think there might be some conflating of the RV coefficient as a descriptive statistic and as a test statistic in a test of modularity.  It *is* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from a landmark configuration comprising two modules, one of which contains only one landmark.  The one-landmark covariance matrix would be a 2 x 2 matrix for 2d landmarks or a 3 x 3 matrix for 3d landmarks, so covariances do exist in these matrices.  But even this is a distraction.  The RV coefficient was introduced by Escoufier in 1973, not with landmarks in mind.  It *is also* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from two variables, each with covariances matrices that are single values: variances.  The RV coefficient should be the square of the correlation coefficient between the variables in such cases, which is why the RV coefficient has intuitive appeal as a multivariate generalization of correlation.
> > > >
> > > > However, a test of modularity using the RV coefficient as a test statistic randomizes combinations of landmarks within modules, which is the same as randomizing the locations of variances and covariances within a covariance matrix, without changing the covariances.  But the randomization is constrained such that x, y, and possibly z covariances within landmarks  cannot be changed (the coordinates are not randomized between landmarks).  Although one *could* calculate an RV coefficient in every random permutation that assigns a landmark randomly to be a one-landmark module, the distribution of RV coefficients from this process would be meaningless for evaluating any null hypothesis about modularity. > > > > > > > > Simulating shapes is typically accomplished with what is called the perturbation model (see Goodall 1991; Dryden and Mardia 1996, etc.). What one does is to simulate random noise at all pk landmark-coordinates, which is then added to a mean shape. Doing this repeatedly results in a sample of random shapes around the mean.  So yes, one requires the mean shape.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > However, it is important to recognize that this process draws samples of random variables from a multivariate normal distribution all at once, not one variable at a time. That requires both the mean, and a covariance matrix from which the MVN distribution is defined.  The mean is easy: that is the mean shape. Generating a valid covariance matrix is rather more involved (and this is where the quote from my paper comes back in).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Procedurally, one may want a certain level of covariance within modules and a different level among modules. That is easy to represent as a square, symmetric matrix. But it may not be a valid covariance matrix (i.e., it may not be positive definite). If not, then the matrix is singular, cannot be inverted, and thus, cannot be used to define the MVN distribution from which random shapes are obtained. So in practice, one generates the desired matrix, and if it is not a valid covariance matrix, one then finds the closest valid covariance matrix to it. There are many ways of doing this, but a useful one is the ‘nearPD’ function in the Matrix library (this uses the classic algorithm of Higham 2002).

Folks,

Mike and I made very clear recommendations on this topic nearly a year ago.  For these rehashed questions now, our answers have not changed. It makes no sense to evaluate covariation among pairs of landmarks in the manner being proposed.

It does not matter whether such things were done in a prior paper: there are many misapplications of analytical tools in the literature, and still more ‘new’ methods that are not properly vetted prior to publication (and should not have been proposed for general use). Additionally, verbal rationalization without formal mathematical proof or numerical validation cannot justify inappropriate use of methods. The Klingenberg quote from the last email was precisely that: it was a thought experiment and rationalization from that (it was not based on formal mathematical or numerical observation). But importantly, one should not use that statement as justification to press on with an inappropriate method: that was not what Klingenberg was trying to say (though that is how the email author took it).

The issue is simple, and has been known since the 1980s. Landmark configurations require registration before shape and shape variation can be evaluated. Even though landmarks are in the same ‘scale’ they cannot be evaluated in their original, as non-shape variation is present. But the registration process, by definition, will cause landmarks to be interdependent. That will affect the subsequent perceived variances and covariances of landmarks (NOTE: not of the shapes!). Therefore, investigating landmark covariance pair by pair makes no logical sense; just as evaluating landmark variance one at a time does not make sense.

Importantly, this problem is the case with ALL superimposition approaches that are in current use: Procrustes superimposition, Resistant Fit, Baseline superimposition, etc. The path forward for this particular application would be the derivation of an alternative weighted superimposition that accounts for this issue, and this requires having an appropriate model against which the superimposition is conditioned (and to date no formal method gets us there to my satisfaction).

Again, what is being discussed (evaluating pairwise landmark covariance) should not be done.  Our recommendation has not changed.

Dean

Dear Prof. Mike,

Thank you for the response. My question is exactly about taking your response in Feb further and ask "Do I really consider that a problem?".

Here is my reasoning why separate standardization indeed is a problem:

If we are comparing the association between body height and weight and between icecream sale and day-time temperature, we do no stop at covariance but rather scale the covariance by sqrt of product of variance since the variables are not on the same scale. But for Procrustes coordinates, they are on the same scale. The scaling step in RV coef does not help much as it does in the icecream example but complicates the issue since GPA influences landmark covariance differntially as a global approach to minize overall variance.

If the above reasoning is in the correct direction, it is implicitly suggesting that we are trying to recover clusters of the original configurations. So we are worried about the impact of changing landmark covariance after GPA. But what if we are to identify clusters of shape of the original configurations after GPA? Some background on this question is from the following statement in page 123 of Klingenberg's 2021 paper "How Exactly Did the Nose Get That Long?": "If the goal is to find a method that represents the covariance structure of the original data, Procrustes superimposition is inherently a poor choice of method because it focuses on shape only and omits all non-shape components of variation. If the goal of the simulation is to extract shape variation, discrepancies between the simulated data and the Procrustes-superimposed configurations are not a problem." This seems to suggest if our aim is to find clusters based on shape data, then the fact that GPA changes landmark variances differentially does not matter much. This is where I get confused.

Thank you for your interest!

Generating a valid covariance matrix is rather more involved (and this is where the quote from my paper comes back in).

> > > > > > > >

But it may not be a valid covariance matrix (i.e., it may not be positive definite). If not, then the matrix is singular, cannot be inverted, and thus, cannot be used to define the MVN distribution from which random shapes are obtained. So in practice, one generates the desired matrix, and if it is not a valid covariance matrix, one then finds the closest valid covariance matrix to it. There are many ways of doing this, but a useful one is the ‘nearPD’ function in the Matrix library (this uses the classic algorithm of Higham 2002).
